title: The first council
hookLine: elders gather at Rajagaha after the Buddha's death: Ananda recites the discourses, Upali the discipline (Vinaya, Cullavagga 11)
carry: held by many mouths, not just one memory

lines: NOW WE CAN DO AS WE LIKE.
cards: The Buddha has died, and the monks on the road are weeping. One old monk named Subhadda tells them to stop. Don't grieve, he says.
We're rid of that great ascetic who was always telling us what's proper and what isn't. Now we can do as we like. The elder Mahakassapa hears it, and he doesn't forget it.
In the Vinaya, the book of monastic discipline, it is this remark that sets him to work. If the teaching isn't gathered now, he reasons, people like Subhadda will decide what it was.

teach.b: Mahakassapa proposes that the elders recite the teaching and the discipline together, before anything false can take root. The Vinaya says five hundred elders were chosen to meet at Rajagaha for the rains.
Ananda had been at the Buddha's side for years and had heard him teach again and again, but he was not yet fully awakened.
The text says he worked hard through the night before the council, and as he lay down to rest, before his head reached the pillow, his mind was freed. He walked into the council as one of the elders.
Mahakassapa doesn't ask for speeches. He asks questions, one at a time.

teach.h: UPALI ON RULES, ANANDA ON DISCOURSES.
teach.b: To Upali, a former barber who had become an expert in the monastic rules: where was the first rule laid down? About whom? In what case?
Upali answers, and the discipline is recited. Then to Ananda: where was this discourse given? To whom?
Ananda answers, and the discourses are recited.
The Pali name for the gathering is sangiti, a chanting together.

It wasn't a debate over new ideas. It was a room full of people saying the same words aloud, checking them against each other, so that the teaching would be held by many mouths and not just one memory.
Some scholars ask how much of this account is history and how much is later telling. The tradition remembers it as the moment the teaching was gathered in, so it could be handed on.

how: Theravada monks still recite texts together in chanting sessions, and the tradition looks back to this first council as the moment its teachings were gathered and fixed.

o: a chanting together, a communal recital
a vote to choose the order's next leader

games.q: the first council: tap the pairs.
p: now we can do as we like

s: the first council debated new teachings
it was a sangiti, a chanting together: the elders recited what the Buddha had taught and checked it aloud.
Ananda was fully awakened only just before the council
the text says his mind was freed as he lay down to rest, before his head reached the pillow.
Upali answered on the discipline; Ananda answered on the discourses.

games.q: you're Mahakassapa. the Buddha has just died, and an old monk tells the others they're finally free to do as they like. what do you do?
o: rebuke him on the spot and move on.
call the elders to recite the teaching together.
games.why: he remembers the remark and proposes that the elders chant the teaching and discipline together, before what is false can spread. the council grows out of one careless sentence.

practice: Choose something you carry by heart, a verse, a poem, a saying from someone who raised you, and say it once quietly, then again more slowly, hearing each word.
Notice which words you're sure of and which ones wobble; that's how the elders checked their memory, by saying it aloud.

wordCard.voice: Sangiti. Elders gathered after the Buddha's death to recite his teaching and his rules aloud, together. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali: a chanting together, a recital. the word used for the Buddhist councils.

carryVoice: Your line: held by many mouths, not just one memory. It all grew from one careless remark. Day eight hundred fifty-one, done.

sources.ref: Vinaya, Cullavagga 11 (the council of the five hundred)
